speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: asked the Minister for Education in view of the results of the Joint Autonomous Universities Graduate Employment Survey 2024, whether the Ministry will consider further measures to boost the proportion of fresh graduates securing full-time permanent jobs after graduation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Employment rates are affected by various factors such as economic and labour market conditions.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The employment rates of fresh graduates from Autonomous Universities (AUs) have remained broadly stable over the decade, with some year-to-year fluctuations due to cyclical changes.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The labour market saw a strong recovery in 2021 and 2022 post-COVID.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In comparison, while the labour market was still tight, there was lower hiring demand and fewer job vacancies in 2024.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We also observed some graduates taking longer to secure full-time employment in 2024.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: These may have contributed to the reported decrease in full-time permanent employment rate and increase in the unemployment rate of graduates from our AUs at six months post-graduation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Even as there was a broad decline in full-time permanent employment rates, some clusters such as Health Sciences and Business continued to see strong employment outcomes.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This indicates that employers continue to value the skills of our graduates.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It also reflects the Government’s commitment to creating good jobs, especially in the growth sectors.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Beyond cyclical fluctuations, we will continue to monitor broader social trends, such as evolving market demand, changing job preferences and aspirations, including more work flexibility and higher salary expectations, that may also affect the employment of our graduates upon graduation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Apart from the Graduate Employment Survey, which tracks employment outcomes six months after graduation, the Government also monitors medium-term outcomes of our graduates through periodic labour market surveys.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: These continuous efforts will enable our curriculum to remain relevant and responsive to market demand.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The AUs will continue to engage industry partners to organise industry talks and career fairs to expose students to emerging sector trends, in-demand skills and connect them with potential employers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Alongside the broad-based employment support and career guidance offered to all students and graduates, personalised career coaching is also available at the respective AUs' Career Centres.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Graduates who require further support in their job search may reach out to the Career Centres, even after graduation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: They may also tap on the career matching services and online resources offered by Workforce Singapore and the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC’s) Employment and Employability Institute (e2i).

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I thank the Minister of State for the reply.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, I note the Minister of State's reply that there are cyclical factors, but I wonder whether there are also structural factors at play in some of the data and trends that we are observing.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because compared to pre-COVID levels, full-time employment of graduates did go up sharply and exceeded pre-COVID levels in 2021 and 2022, as the Minister of State has also noted in her reply, as we recovered from COVID.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In Business, it is about five percentage points lower in 2024 compared to pre-COVID levels; in the Built Environment, seven percentage points lower in 2024; and in Engineering, five percentage points lower compared to pre-COVID levels.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And one would imagine that these are growing sectors and there should be growing demand for our graduates in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Minister of State what is driving this trend and are there structural factors at play?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The second clarification also on the basis of my first question, have these observations given the Ministry of Education (MOE) any cause to look at and adjust its fundamental assumptions in the determination of the number of places available in each course of study in each university going forward?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To put things in context, the Graduate Employment Survey provides a snapshot of graduate employment outcomes approximately six months after graduation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The employment rates for Singaporeans aged 25 to 29 have remained broadly stable over the decade along with low long-term unemployment rates.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This suggests that our graduates do not have prolonged job search difficulties.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are fluctuations in sectoral employment rates and these are to be expected given the cyclical nature of the economy and the labour market.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will continue to work with the sector agencies to monitor these outcomes to see if there is a more persistent trend.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For specific sectors, such as the Built Environment and Manufacturing, and in addition to the cyclical effects, these have also tended to be sectors that have faced greater challenges attracting graduates into the sector.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are ongoing efforts by the sector agencies and industry to review how they can better attract graduates into these sectors.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This takes into account the employment prospects of graduates from various disciplines alongside national manpower needs and of course, the students' interests.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can I just ask two clarifications from the Minister of State?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is with regard to the higher median salary in the third question of my original PQ.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Just as the hon Member, Mr Xie had highlighted, is there a skills gap, because there is greater demand in certain sectors for jobs, and employers are facing difficulty filling those.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the same time, our fresh graduates are facing problems.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And also, what is driving the higher median salary?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Over the years we have also adjusted the university places in courses that we deem to have higher market demand, as well as high interest of our students.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, actually, in terms of absolute numbers of our fresh graduates from the AUs, it has grown over the last five years.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And we see that more are going to the growth sectors with higher salaries.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Hence, there is this increase in median salaries of our graduates as a whole.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To the Member's question, whether there could be skills gap, our universities always work with the sector agencies and industry leaders to look at the skills required for the jobs that are available today.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We try as well to project ahead what might be the future skills.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It takes about three to four years in the universities for our students before they graduate.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And it is therefore important that we always update the curriculum to make sure that our graduates are equipped with the relevant skills by the time they graduate.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And the remaining one-third of this group that had job offers reject the job offers for various reasons.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, the texture is not as straightforward as what is seen.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will continue to do our best to support every graduate out there to be able to find a job that suits their needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In 2020 to 2022, particularly during the pandemic period, there was a sudden surge of high demand in professional services, including and especially in infocomm technology (ICT).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And as a result, many in the last couple of years have embarked on Computer Science and ICT-related programmes in our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, as we can see, in the last 15 to 18 months, there is a bit of consolidation, rationalisation and restructuring, exacerbated by generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) in this sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And many of these graduates are coming out in the next three years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How is MOE helping, and integrating possibly the Ministry of Manpower, to overcome this fear or the apprehensions of our upcoming graduates?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I recall seeing some of these headline figures, some companies offering $8,000 and above for fresh graduates from our universities going into this sector.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The market has kind of stabilised in more recent times.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We know that there are some graduates in ICT who are able to get employed very quickly and still being offered very high salaries.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But the demand has tapered and so, we are also seeing some graduates who feel that perhaps if they wait a little bit more, they might be able to still find a job with similarly attractive high salaries.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I think there is transition going on now.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We do ask our graduates who are still looking for a job to speak to career coaches and keep in touch with the Career Centres in the universities so that they are more updated on the industry trends.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: On graduates who are in ICT, there is actually still a very high demand, although we also know out there in the market, there is some churn, some consolidation, some retrenchments as well.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, it is understandable that the hiring of our graduates in this sector has softened.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It means that our graduates from ICT actually do have the flexibility to go to jobs that are in adjacent sectors too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My two clarifications will really be a follow-on from the question I asked last month on the Polytechnic Graduate Employment Survey 2024, which also showed fewer graduates securing full-time permanent jobs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister for Education gave an extensive reply in response to that PQ.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first clarification for the Minister of State is whether the Minister of State sees the latest Graduate Employment Survey as reflective of a perhaps longer-term secular trend of graduates at the university level finding it harder to get jobs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the concern is, does the Ministry assess this potentially to be a secular issue, going forward?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second point is with regard to the reply that the Minister for Education gave vis-a-vis the earlier PQ that I filed in February on polytechnic graduates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister also made reference to university graduates and the things that are required to ensure that they get not just a good salary and a fulfilling job at the point of entry post graduation, but also through their careers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And the two points he made was first closer industry university collaboration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think the Minister of State referred to that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, it is not a question of doing one extra module or two extra modules in an adjacent subject, for example, like human resources (HR), but more directed courses to ensure that in the event a graduate cannot find a place in his primary course of study, there is something parallel, which potentially could provide good job opportunities for that graduate.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For the two supplementary questions, I will answer the second one first.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Certainly, yes, we believe in a broad-based education for our students.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: From the time they enter our mainstream education, we already start equipping them with different sets of skills and with some specialisation as they go into our tertiary education institutions.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And even in the tertiary education institutions, students actually have the ability to choose various other modules beyond their specialised courses, so that they will have also adjacent skills that help broaden their employability.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And certainly, we will continue to review the course syllabus and offerings to our graduates.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We do this in close partnership with the industry and the sector agencies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Actually, beyond the technical skills and the professional skills, it is also important to equip our graduates, whether from polytechnics, the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) or universities, with useful life skills, so that they are able to navigate uncertainties and also be able to pick up new knowledge and skills beyond graduation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, lifelong learning, getting our graduates to understand that what they have learned or picked up in the first 15 years of their education, while it is enough for them to be able or for most of them to be able to get jobs, they still need to upgrade themselves.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And if they are in a sector that is disrupted due to external environmental conditions, then all the more it is important for them to have the relevant life skills and the gumption to pick up new skills.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: On the first question, Mr Pritam Singh made reference to polytechnic graduates.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Minister for Education gave a very long reply.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But I would like to say that while there was a decline in the graduate employment for that group, there are also more and more polytechnic graduates whom we see would want to upgrade themselves beyond a diploma.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: That also affects the employment outcomes for this group.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, I think it is useful for us not to over-generalise the graduate employment of our polytechnic and our university students together.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And to the question of whether it has become harder for university graduates to find a job, I explained quite extensively earlier on.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: What we see is that the trend has been quite stable.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Rest assured that we will continue to look out for our graduates' employment outcomes and we are ready to make adjustments so that graduates will be able to find fulfilling jobs that meet their aspirations and needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the Minister of State may have misunderstood my first supplementary question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was not on polytechnic graduates per se.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was about the longer-term structural trends with regard to university graduates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I referenced polytechnic graduates because the reply that Minister gave earlier in February also include the reference, not just to polytechnic graduates, but ITE graduates, university graduates as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, the first supplementary question was essentially about the longer-term secular trend given the numbers coming out of the Graduate Employment Survey since 2022.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Does the Minister of State or the Ministry see it as a longer-term structure, secular trend in a particular direction?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Speaker, Sir, I thought it is a very useful discussion today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I would just like to make a few points in response to various Members' comments and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Because yesterday we hear a suggestion for us that we should just increase the number of graduates so long as they can perhaps meet some benchmarks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And today's discussion actually brings us back to where exactly we want to go.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not about how many graduates we produce a year that matters most at 18 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some countries, they produce over 90% of their cohort as graduates and they have quite poor employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some developed countries in Europe have only 20% going to universities and many of them going to trade schools, and they have very good employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The crux of the matter is what are the skill sets that we are equipping them with.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And it is not just about having everybody go to university, because we all want to go after the paper chase.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The second point is that indeed we must always monitor the long-term secular trends and the short-term cyclical trends.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For us to produce a graduate, whether in polytechnic or university, it takes us three to four years, so we cannot be responding to the short-term trends always.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And that is how we must work closely with our industry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, I would just like to register the point that together with yesterday's discussion, it is not about chasing the numbers of graduates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Certainly, it is about equipping our graduates regardless of their age with the relevant skills.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I actually really hope we can get to the next block of questions.
